title: All shall be well
hook: Julian is told that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations of Divine Love 27)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shu, spared because his body fit none of the world's measures. Your line was the hidden gift. Did a limit spare you anything, or nothing? Today, a sick woman's question, and the answer she heard. Day seven hundred thirty.

All shall be well. Said fast, it can sound like it'll be fine, the kind of thing said over a shoulder on the way out of a room, when nobody knows what else to say. But the woman who wrote it down didn't hear it in passing. She heard it in her sickbed. Julian of Norwich, whom this path met with a hazelnut in her palm, writes that she was so ill the people around her thought she was dying. And she wasn't asking for comfort. She was asking a hard question. Today: what she asked, and what she heard back.
screen: `SAID FAST, IT SOUNDS LIKE: IT'LL BE FINE.` → `JULIAN HEARD IT IN THE BED.` → `SHE WAS ASKING A HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In chapter twenty-seven of her Revelations of Divine Love, Julian says she wondered why God, in all his foreseeing wisdom, didn't stop sin at the very beginning. Because then, she thought, all would have been well. It's the old why, asked straight, by someone in pain. Second, the answer. She doesn't get a reason. She hears that sin was behovely, an old word for fitting, something that had its place. And then the line, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tone. Julian notices how it was said. In her telling, the words came very tenderly, with no blame laid on her, nor on any who shall be saved. Not a lecture. Not a correction for asking. Just a promise, said kindly to a person who had dared the question. Fourth, the tense. Listen to it again: shall. Not all is well. All shall be. Julian doesn't pretend the world in front of her is fine. And she doesn't stop asking either. In the chapters that follow she keeps pressing how it could ever be made well, with so much harm in the world. Later she is told, in paraphrase, that she'll see it herself: that all manner of thing shall be well. So the line isn't an answer that ends the question. It's a promise that keeps her company while the question stays open. Some Christians who read Julian hold it that way, and some readers take it simply as a line from a woman who asked honestly, and was answered gently.
screen: `WHY WASN'T SIN STOPPED AT THE START?` · `NO REASON. A PROMISE.` · `SAID TENDERLY, WITH NO BLAME.` · `SHALL, NOT IS.` · then, large: `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind one thing that is not well right now. In your life, or someone else's. Let it be what it is; you don't need to fix it or explain it. Then, once, silently and slowly, say Julian's line: all shall be well. Only once. Don't repeat it to drown the hard thing out. Notice how it lands. If it rings true, let it. If it rings false today, let that be honest too. If you pray, you can offer it as Julian heard it, as a promise. If you don't, hold it as a line from a book. The bell holds the time.
All shall be well. Julian's words, heard in sickness, in answer to the question why. Not all is well. All shall be. Today's word.
Your line: all shall be well. Today, when something isn't well, say it once, slowly, without forcing it, and then turn back to what's in front of you. Day seven hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Christians of several churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love, and her line all shall be well is sometimes said or sung in prayer services and at times of grief.

notes: Quotation from Grace Warrack's 1901 edition, chapter 27: confirm the exact wording and punctuation of 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' in her text.

Chapter 27 paraphrased: Julian wondered why the beginning of sin was not prevented, 'for then, methought, all should have been well'; the reply that sin is behovely, said 'full tenderly', with no blame to her or to any. Confirm.
'Behovely' glossed as 'fitting, something that had its place'; Warrack's modernization may read 'It behoved that there should be sin'. Confirm the script's wording against her edition.
Chapters 2–3: Julian's illness, those around her believing she was dying. Her age and the year are left out under the claims rule.
Chapter 32 paraphrased: 'thou shalt see thyself that all manner of thing shall be well'. Confirm chapter.
'Christians who read Julian often hold it that way' and howItsDone 'many churches' are soft generalizations; cut if a reviewer prefers. The hazelnut was day 88.

Audit: 'no blame on her, or on anyone' overstated chapter 27, which says no blame to her 'nor to any that shall be saved'; teach and match pair narrowed to match the text.
